Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' These items describe opposing levels of verbal access to the trauma memory and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's current self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked memory disturbance items ('some moments are extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'there are parts of the event I simply cannot remember'). Although fragmented trauma memory can coexist with disclosure, the wording 'very easily' is hard to reconcile with this level of fragmentation in the same profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
issues.explanation: Across Memory and Negative Appraisals, reporting that one can talk about the event 'very easily' sits in tension with the appraisal 'If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it.' Patients may force themselves to discuss trauma despite distress, but these two statements point in opposite directions and are difficult to integrate clinically without additional context.

vignette:
Kalani had always been the calm center of the storm. For thirty years as a community organizer, he had navigated heated town halls and mediated bitter disputes, his steady presence a balm on frayed nerves. But for the last six months, ever since the screech of tires and the explosive shatter of glass, that center had collapsed. The accident happened on a Tuesday afternoon. He was driving to a meeting, humming along to the radio, when a delivery truck barreled through a red light. The impact was a violent, metallic scream. Kalani's memory of the event is a tattered cloth, riddled with holes. He has no recollection of the crash itself, a terrifying blankness where the most critical seconds should be. What remains are vivid, looping fragments: the truck driver, a young man with a face contorted in fury, storming over to his window and screaming that it was all his fault; the cold, dismissive tone of the first police officer on the scene, whose uniform badge seemed to fill Kalani's entire field of vision.

These fragments have become their own kind of torment. Because he cannot remember the moment of impact, he is haunted by the possibility that the screaming driver was right. This gap in his memory has become fertile ground for a deep, corrosive self-blame. He spends hours trying to reconstruct the timeline, certain that if he could just remember, he would uncover the mistake he must have made. This conviction that the event happened because of how he acted has reshaped his past into a story of his own failure. The more he blames himself, the harder it becomes to approach the memory at all; the thought of it is so laden with shame that his mind recoils, leaving the gaps unfilled and the questions unanswered. He knows what happened, in a factual sense, but when he tries to speak of it, he finds he is unable to find the words, as if his own guilt has stolen his voice.

The world now feels like a landscape of hidden threats. The intrusive, unwanted thought of the driver's angry face can surface without warning, a memory fragment that acts as its own trigger. This internal cue system is matched by an external one. The sight of a police uniform on the street causes an immediate, full-body reaction-a cold sweat, a racing heart-that feels utterly disconnected from the present moment. He has come to see his body as an enemy, convinced it keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is rationally safe. This sense of physical betrayal is most acute at work. During a recent planning meeting about a new community garden, a resident raised his voice in frustration, his tone not even truly aggressive, just firm. For Kalani, the sound was a direct echo of the accident. The anger in the room, however mild, instantly confirmed his own appraisal of himself as incompetent and at fault. He felt a wave of shame so intense it was paralyzing, a certainty that everyone could see his weakness.

This constant feeling of being judged and blameworthy has made him hyper-attuned to any sign of conflict. He now scans every room, every interaction, for the slightest expression of anger, which in turn makes him more likely to be triggered. A raised voice doesn't just startle him; it launches him into a spiral of self-recrimination. It is in these moments that he feels most profoundly what he describes as being "dead inside." The vibrant, engaged man who could hold a room together has been replaced by someone hollowed out by a shame he cannot articulate and a physical terror he cannot control. His work, once his calling, has become a source of dread. He has started cancelling meetings, delegating tasks he once loved, all to avoid the possibility of confrontation.

Kalani came to therapy because he could no longer stand the emotional numbness. He misses the man he used to be-the one who felt connected to his community, who believed in his own capacity for good. He is terrified that this hollowed-out version is all that is left. The accident may have broken his body, but it is the unrelenting cycle of memory, blame, and fear that he feels is now breaking his soul.
